source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1985/2010) Rapid decision making on the fire ground: the original study plus a postscript
finding: Founding study. Interviews with fireground commanders about non-routine incidents. Most decision points were handled by recognising the situation as a typical prototype and a typical action, with no comparison of options.
numbers: 26 experienced fireground commanders, mean 23 years experience. 156 decision points probed. Under 12% showed simultaneous comparison of two or more options. Over 80% used direct recognition of situation and action.
quote: In over 80% of the decision points, the strategy was for the FGCs to use their experience to directly identify the situation as typical
limits: Read as the published abstract via Crossref, not the full text. Retrospective interviews, one domain, no control group, classification of decision points by the authors. The 1985 study was unpublished until 2010; the 1986 Human Factors Society proceedings paper (pp. 576-580) is the short version.
agent_relevance: Mode choice: a strong expert default is one workable option, not a comparison. Our agent should not force option comparison where a typical case is recognised.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground, Proc. Human Factors Society 30, 576-580
finding: Short first publication of the RPD model; the DTIC technical report is ADA199492. I could not open either text this session (DTIC returned 403 and an HTML page).
numbers: Not read. Numbers above come from the 2010 abstract of the same data.
limits: Not opened; cited by title only.
agent_relevance: Use the 2010 version as the citable record of the numbers.

source: Klein (2008) Naturalistic decision making, Human Factors 50(3)
finding: Klein's own account of the NDM approach. NDM began in the 1980s to study decisions in real settings. The framework stresses that experience lets people categorise situations fast and decide well.
numbers: No figures in the abstract. NDM movement began at a Dayton, Ohio conference in 1989 and led to Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok (1993) Decision Making in Action (per the Wikipedia NDM page).
quote: The NDM framework emphasizes the role of experience in enabling people to rapidly categorize situations to make effective decisions.
limits: Abstract only. Written by the theory's founder, so it is advocacy as well as review.
agent_relevance: Treat RPD as one part of a field that studies expert decisions in context; do not expect lab-style effect sizes.

source: Wikipedia: Recognition primed decision
finding: Core model: generate one course of action, check it against the situation, take the first one not rejected. Three variants. V1: situation and action known (if-then). V2: diagnose an unknown situation, then act. V3: situation understood, response unknown, so mentally simulate actions and stop at the first that seems to work.
numbers: No numbers. Page carries a needs-more-citations tag; its only source is Klein (1998) Sources of Power, pp. 1-30. It lists chess players among groups using RPD.
limits: Weak secondary source. States the limits: needs extensive experience; recognition and modelling fail in unusual or misidentified situations.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean three-mode structure: match and act, diagnose then act, simulate then act. Maps to mode choice in our schema.

source: Wikipedia: Naturalistic decision making
finding: NDM history and reference list: Klein et al. (1993), Klein (2008), Zsambok and Klein (1997), Johnson and Raab (2003) take-the-first, Todd and Gigerenzer (2001), Newell, Lagnado and Shanks (2007).
numbers: No empirical numbers. Says 'Expertise is crucial for using RPD' and gives the 1989 Dayton conference origin.
limits: Short page; used only to find citations.
agent_relevance: Points to the take-the-first and adaptive-toolbox literature as the formal neighbours of RPD.

source: Klein (2021) The RPD model: criticisms and confusions, Psychology Today
finding: Klein answers six criticisms. RPD has two parts: fast pattern matching and slower mental simulation, which he equates with Kahneman's System 1 and 2. It is not limited to time pressure. He says it is falsifiable: inexperienced people use the RPD tactic less than half the time, and in chess (Klein et al. 1995) skilled players' first option was high quality, which random first options would not be.
numbers: Inexperienced decision makers use RPD 'less than half the time' (no N given). Klein says the work has been replicated several times, without citing which.
quote: the RPD model has two components
limits: Blog post by the model's author. No data tables, no named critics. Replication claims are not itemised, so I cannot verify them.
agent_relevance: RPD is defined by a match step plus a simulate step. Our scaffold should keep a check-before-commit step, not only first-match.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree, American Psychologist 64, 515-526
finding: Joint paper by the heuristics-and-biases and NDM camps. Intuition can be trusted when two conditions hold: a regular, predictable environment, and a real chance to learn its regularities. Confidence is not a guide to accuracy.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract shown.
quote: Subjective experience is not a reliable indicator of judgment accuracy.
limits: Abstract only. The full text (not opened) covers fireground commanders, chess and cases where intuition fails.
agent_relevance: Gives the gate for mode choice: use the fast mode only where the task type is regular and the agent has seen many similar cases; never use stated confidence as the gate.

source: Chassy, Lahaye, Didierjean, Gobet (2023) Intuition in chess: a study with world-class players, Psychological Research 87, 2380-2389
finding: Players of four skill levels judged positions after 5 seconds. Better players made smaller evaluation errors, so quick pattern recognition improves with skill. Errors rose with position complexity, which the authors say contradicts Dreyfus's claim that experts grasp a situation without parts.
numbers: N=63 (15 female): candidate masters 14 (mean Elo 2106), masters 15 (2314), international 17 (2486), world-class 17 (2691). Mean error 1.58, 1.52, 1.39, 1.17. F(3,59)=14.56, eta squared 0.425. Elo explains 44% of error variance (r=0.664). Simple 1.31 vs complex 1.50, F(1,59)=34.27. Response time did not differ by skill (F(3,59)=0.713). 56 positions.
limits: Only 5-second evaluation, no move choice, no time pressure in play. Four positions per balance cell. Complexity defined by piece count. The Elo 4366 zero-error line is extrapolation.
agent_relevance: Fast recognition is real and skill-graded, but it degrades as complexity rises. Gate the fast mode on how typical and simple the case is.

source: Vidulich and Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications
finding: Archival chess data against an RPD-only view. Grandmasters at blitz made more and larger blunders than in standard games. Within standard games, elite players spent time unevenly: fast in the opening, slow in the middle, hurried before time control, and fast moves under time shortage were worse.
numbers: Study 1: 20 grandmasters at Wijk aan Zee (1998-99), about 3 min per move standard vs about 7.5 s blitz. Blunder proportion 0.20 to 0.27; mean blunder size 0.98 to 1.45 pawns. Expected Blunder per Move 0.20 to 0.38; higher in blitz for 18 of 20 players. Losers 0.39 vs winners 0.15 in standard games. Study 2: 11 World Championship matches, 7 champions; moves 11-20 averaged over 6 min, last five before time control under 2 min.
quote: intuit when feasible and deliberate when necessary
limits: Archival; time spent on the opponent's move was not modelled. Read about 100,000 of 119,588 characters. Authors argue against RPD as the primary basis of expertise; Klein would reply that RPD includes a simulate step.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a mode switch by stakes and time available: experts intuit when feasible and deliberate when necessary. Do not run one mode always.

source: Vidulich and Tsang (2026), as quoted on earlier chess time-pressure work (Chabris and Hearst 2003; Chang and Lane 2016; Moxley et al. 2012; Burns 2004; Gobet and Simon)
finding: Secondary account only. Chabris and Hearst: grandmasters made more and larger blunders in 15-minute rapid games than in standard games. Chang and Lane: even in blitz, stronger players took long on selected moves. Moxley et al.: players changed their first move more in hard positions. Burns left 19 to 36% of variance unexplained. Montero: Kasparov's simultaneous-game rating fell from 2750 to 2646, which is substantial.
numbers: Grandmaster Elo 2530-2790 (Chabris and Hearst). Kasparov rating drop 2750 to 2646. Burns unexplained variance 19-36%.
limits: These primary papers were not opened by me; the numbers are as quoted in the 2026 paper.
agent_relevance: Speed explains only part of chess skill, so 'fast means recognition' is not a safe inference for the agent.

source: Calderwood, Klein, Crandall (1988) Time pressure, skill, and move quality in chess, American Journal of Psychology 101, 481-493
finding: Named by Vidulich and Tsang as a lab study of chess under time pressure that supports the intuition view. Not opened; I record no numbers.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Needs a second pass when full text access exists.
agent_relevance: Candidate evidence that move quality holds up under speed for experts.

source: Klein, Wolf, Militello, Zsambok (1995) Characteristics of skilled option generation in chess, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 62, 63-69
finding: Per Klein (2021): skilled players' first-generated option was of high quality, which he uses as a falsifiable test of RPD. Publisher pages blocked (403), so not read.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Klein's own summary only.
agent_relevance: The chess test of 'first option is good' is the closest direct evidence for this subfield; it needs to be read in full.

source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies, JMIR Biomedical Engineering
finding: LLM test of an RPD prompt. The prompt told the model to check whether the case matches a familiar typical case, simulate whether the usual action works, and revise if not. It beat a default prompt on overall accuracy, mainly by fixing self-care advice.
numbers: 45 real vignettes (2 emergency, 30 nonemergency, 13 self-care), 10 models, 3 prompts, 10 runs each, 13,500 assessments. Accuracy default 63.3%, RPD 67.6%, data-frame 66.7% (odds ratios 2.26 and 2.05, p<.001). Self-care 13.4% to 29.8% (RPD). GPT-4.1 self-care advice 0% to 43.8%. GPT-5.2 self-care stayed 0%. 88% of errors were over-triage. Fleiss kappa 0.766 default, 0.717 RPD. At least one correct in 10 runs: 73.1%, 82.2%.
limits: One domain, only 2 emergency cases, ChatGPT models only, no human users, more output tokens. The gain mostly moves the model away from over-triage; it may be a prompt-format effect rather than a recognition effect.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence: an RPD-style prompt can help where the default over-escalates, and the gain was larger for reasoning models. It did not help the newest model on self-care.

source: Thanasuan and Mueller (2014) Crossword expertise as recognitional decision making: an artificial intelligence approach, Frontiers in Psychology 5:1018
finding: Computational model of expert crossword solving built on recognitional decision making. Fast, fluent memory retrieval explains experts; error correction and backtracking mattered less. Authors say classic RPD needs amending for domains that demand exact answers: the decision becomes 'do I know it?' and how to continue search.
numbers: Humans: no novice finished in 25 min (23.9 words, SD 9.4; 23.1 correct). All experts finished in 5.3 min (SD 2.5) with 77.2 of 78 correct (SD 1.5). Eight model variants; only the two with high recovery and fast retrieval matched expert timing and accuracy and beat all novices. Optimising strategy only slightly better than random.
limits: One puzzle. Models fitted to a small human sample. Not about a choice between actions.
agent_relevance: Boundary case: when only an exact answer works, RPD becomes retrieve, test, and keep searching. A useful shape for answer-checking tasks.

source: Naturalistic decision-making in sport: how current advances into the RPD model offer insights (2022), Frontiers; citing Macquet (2020)
finding: RPD has been applied to many sports. In Macquet's review most expert decisions were simple matches. Rugby coaches with less time pressure decided more by deliberate analysis (Collins et al. 2016).
numbers: Macquet (2020): 60-81% of expert decisions simple match, 13-28% diagnosis, 3-24% evaluating a course of action. Prior sport work: preferred first option chosen in about 80% of decisions (uncited in the page).
limits: Mostly qualitative first-person interview studies. The 80% claim is uncited in this source.
agent_relevance: Mix of modes varies with time pressure: more time gave more analysis. The agent's mode should depend on time and stakes.

source: Le Menn et al. (2019) Handball goalkeeper intuitive decision-making: a naturalistic case study, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: An expert goalkeeper's accounts were coded against RPD. Recognition processes did not change with thrower distance, but micro-decisions did.
numbers: 83 short accounts, 419 units of salient features, three RPD process types, four micro-decision types. Distance affected micro-decision categories but not recognition processes.
limits: One goalkeeper. Qualitative coding, no control group.
agent_relevance: Recognition stays stable while the action choice adapts to the situation; match and adapt are separate steps.

source: Community pharmacists' decision-making patterns in clinical prescription checking: a simulation-based study (2025)
finding: Think-aloud coding against RPD. Pharmacists mostly used pattern recognition, and turned analytical when they met an atypical situation. Cue and expectancy processing was consistent; the actions chosen varied and showed hesitancy.
numbers: 12 community pharmacists, deductive thematic analysis. No effect sizes.
limits: Tiny sample, qualitative, simulated task.
agent_relevance: Supports an atypicality trigger for switching from fast to analytic mode.

source: How do surgeons make intraoperative decisions? (2007)
finding: Treats RPD as the intuitive method in surgery: recognise the problem, recall a rule or similar case. Interview evidence says RPD was 'implicit in many' cases. Likely used by experienced surgeons, not novices.
numbers: No counts, sample sizes or percentages reported in the article.
limits: Qualitative; no measured accuracy.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Do not cite it for rates.

source: Deriving the Practice-Primed Decision Model from NDM for acute care nursing research (2019)
finding: Describes RPD as built from interviews with fireground commanders on non-routine fires. A pattern holds cues, expectancies, plausible goals and typical outcomes. After a match, the person projects how the action would play out. Result: the first workable solution.
numbers: No study numbers given.
limits: Derivative model for nursing; no criticisms discussed.
agent_relevance: Good compact definition of what a stored pattern contains: cues, expectancies, goals, typical action.

source: Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox (2016), Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Repeats the headline claim that RPD accounted for 80-90% of firefighters' decisions, and that it could not have been found in the lab because it depends on 10-20 years of experience.
numbers: RPD accounted for 80-90% of firefighter decisions (quoted claim, no table). Experience needed: 10-20 years.
quote: The RPD model accounted for 80-90% of the decisions that firefighters made.
limits: The 80-90% figure is higher than the original 'over 80%' and shows number drift in retellings.
agent_relevance: Quote the original figure (over 80% of 156), not the drifted 80-90%.

source: Raab and Gigerenzer (2015) The power of simplicity: a fast-and-frugal heuristics approach to performance science, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Formal neighbour of RPD: take-the-first. Options are generated in order of learned validity and search stops at the first feasible one. It predicts a negative link between number of options generated and quality; the long-term working memory model predicts a positive link. Moderators: situation, emotion, personality.
numbers: No new numbers in the passages I read. Notes spread to nursing, navigation, law, medicine, consumer choice, engineering.
limits: Review; the underlying Johnson and Raab (2003) paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable, code-friendly rule for fast mode: rank by learned validity, stop at first feasible.

source: Johnson and Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices, OBHDP 91, 215-229
finding: Named across sources as the lab test of take-the-first (more options generated, worse choices) with handball experts. Elsevier pages blocked, so I did not read it and record no numbers.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Needs direct reading; it is the main lab support for first-option quality.

source: Hepler and Feltz (2012) Take the first heuristic, self-efficacy, and decision-making in sport, J. Experimental Psychology: Applied 18, 154-161
finding: Cited in a 2022 Frontiers sport paper's reference list as an extension of take-the-first. Not opened; no findings recorded.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate boundary-condition study (self-efficacy).

source: Ji et al. (2007) A fuzzy logic-based computational recognition-primed decision model, Information Sciences 177, 4338-4353
finding: Named in the crossword paper's reference list as a computational RPD model. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Prior computational implementation to check for how mental simulation was coded.

source: Klein (2021) on computational models of RPD
finding: Klein says RPD is only easy to model if mental simulation is ignored. Reinforcement-learning AI models learn from reward, while people also diagnose what went wrong to build stronger mental models.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Opinion of the model's author.
agent_relevance: A pattern-match-only agent is half of RPD. The other half is a check run before acting.

source: Vidulich and Tsang (2026) practical implication on training
finding: Authors warn that training on repeated exposure, as RPD suggests, may leave experts unprepared for unfamiliar events. Deliberation needs deep organised knowledge. Sullenberger's Hudson landing is offered as effective use of limited time to deliberate.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument, not a test.
agent_relevance: Unusual situations are the known failure point of fast mode. Add an out-of-pattern detector before committing.

source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) model-type and emergency-case results
finding: The two NDM prompts gave larger gains for reasoning models (RPD odds ratio 2.15, p<.001; data-frame 1.70, p=.008). Largest single gain was GPT-4.1 mini with the data-frame prompt, +13 points (95% CI 9.7 to 16.1). Emergency accuracy 100% default, 98% RPD, 99% data-frame.
numbers: Nonemergency accuracy about 82-83% across prompts.
limits: 2 emergency cases make the emergency numbers unstable. The 1-2 point drop on emergencies was not tested.
agent_relevance: An RPD-style prompt may slightly raise the risk of missing rare serious cases; test on rare-event items.
